speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ACTIVITIES OF R.C.M.P. IN LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the importance of the subject and the concern over the situation, I should like to make a statement to the house as to the present position in the strike area in Newfoundland in so far as the R.C.M. police are concerned. I should like to make clear at the outset, as I shall be doing in more detail later on, that at no time have the police acted as strikebreakers, taken sides in the strike, or escorted or attempted to escort anyone through a picket line. They have acted throughout in strict conformity with their duties as police responsible for the protection of property and the maintenance of law and order, and indeed have conducted themselves admirably throughout a long and extremely trying period, and sometimes in the face of great provocation.
The functions of the R.C.M. police in this situation are determined by the provisions of the police contract between Canada and Newfoundland, the relevant provisions of which are paragraphs 4 and 5, which are as follows:
4. The division shall perform in the province such duties and render such services as are ordinarily performed by peace officers in aiding the administration of justice and in carrying into effect the laws of a provincial legislature.
5.	The officer commanding the division shall for the purposes of this agreement act under the direction of the attorney general of the province in aiding the administration of justice in the province and in carrying into effect the laws of the legislature.
A copy of this contract was tabled in the house on February 16.
It is of course the obligation of a police force at all times to enforce the provisions of the Criminal Code. These duties involve normally the investigation of acts of violence which are a breach of the code, such as assault and damage to property, and arresting offenders who commit such acts. It is an unfortunate fact that as a result of the tension and bad feeling engendered in the course of this strike, as between those who wish to continue working and those who wish to prevent anyone from working, cases
of assault and damage to property have been multiplied, thus magnifying the burdens of law enforcement.
The fact that there is a strike, however, does not relieve the police of their responsibilities in this field, but on the contrary imposes upon them extra duties of taking precautions to see that the tension and bad feelings engendered are not in fact allowed to result in general lawlessness and violence. They must protect the public-and this includes those involved in the dispute- against the possibility of excesses arising out of the tense situation.
In addition, under strike conditions there arises the further obligation of enforcing section 366 of the Criminal Code, which deals specifically with picketing and makes it unlawful for anyone engaged in picketing to use violence or threats of violence to any person, or intimidation, or to indulge in disorders. In particular, section 368 makes it unlawful to block or obstruct the highways.
It will thus be seen that under strike conditions the police are bound to be called upon from time to time to perform special duties such, for instance, as to make sure roads are kept open for traffic. Under normal conditions the necessity for such action does not arise, but under strike conditions it is a specific duty they have to perform.
It is apparent that the manner in which the police have discharged their duties must be judged against this background. Regard must be had to the nature of the problems with which they had to deal, the area in which they have had to carry out their duties and the total numbers of the loggers involved and of the police available.
The most troubled area is that of Grand Falls, particularly the Badger district. The Grand Falls area, extending from Gander lake to Millertown, stretches across a front of approximately 75 miles. The area involved extends southward across the island for a distance of 50 to 60 miles. If the Corner Brook district, where about 1,000 of the Bowater company's loggers are out on strike in sympathy with the Anglo-New-foundland Development Company loggers, were included, then the area would be extended by a further 300 miles.
There are many thousands of loggers involved. Indeed, I have seen one estimate
1826	HOUSE OF
Newfoundland-Administration of Justice which puts the number as high as 18,000. I am informed that a substantial number of the 1,000 loggers at Corner Brook, whom I have mentioned, have just moved over to the Badger district to support the strikers in that area. As against this I am advised that the total police strength attending to the strike situation is 143, the majority of whom are employed in the most troubled area around Badger. This strength has recently been supplemented by a group of some 25 from the Newfoundland constabulary, who normally police the city of St. John's and are not part of the R.C.M. police.
As I have stated, the actions of the police in this very difficult situation have been entirely preventive. Their actions have been limited to enforcing the provisions of the Criminal Code against assault, damage to property, acts of violence, obstruction of roads and other similar provisions.
Furthermore, the position of the police as I have described it has been outlined by responsible police officers to the union officials concerned, by whom it has been accepted. In addition the police have been at pains, in all cases where picket lines have been established or where men have gathered on the roads, to explain to them the limits imposed upon their activities by the Criminal Code.
It is an unfortunate fact that since the commencement of this strike, and particularly within the last six weeks, it has been necessary to make a number of arrests and charges. The total number of charges laid in this period has been 202, which have been disposed of as follows: convicted, 71; dismissed, 15; awaiting trial, 75; withdrawn 41.
Since there have been a number of accusations made against the police which have arisen in the main out of three major incidents, I should give here a factual account of what actually took place on those occasions, because the facts demonstrate most clearly that the police have only acted when the provisions of the Criminal Code have been violated.
The first incident was on February 7, when 84 strikers went to two camps in the Badger district at about 3.30 a.m. At the first camp they forced 50 workers out of their building and left them to walk in sub-zero weather to Badger, about 10 miles away. Many of the workers were insufficiently clothed. At this camp they broke windows and furniture and did other damage to property. At the second camp they threatened violence, with the result that 23 loggers decided to leave. As a result of these violations 79 men were arrested and charged.
The second incident took place on March 9. About 45 pickets blocked the main road


leading to Halls Bay. A police patrol went out and persuaded the pickets to cease their obstruction, which they did. On the way back the patrol met a crowd of about 200 on the same road; they radioed for help and on the arrival of reinforcements the crowd opened up and ceased to obstruct the road. On both these occasions on that day, therefore, the police were able to discharge their duties by peaceful persuasion and no arrests were made.
The third incident was last night. At about
5.00	p.m. yesterday the police detachment at Badger reported a crowd of about 250 collecting on the road outside the town. In order to prevent or remove the obstruction the police detail went to the scene and saw that a car which was trying to get through had been stopped by the crowd, its windows had been broken and the car had been forced to turn back. It was also observed that this crowd was armed with sticks, peaveys and bottles. It was established later that one of them was carrying an axe.
A call was sent for a police detail from Grand Falls to help deal with this situation, since the road was blocked. On arrival of a detail of some 50 police, including some members of the Newfoundland constabulary, words were exchanged in which the police clearly indicated that the obstruction could not be allowed to continue and the group must disperse. One of the crowd then swung an axe at one of the leading policemen. The police moved in to arrest him. This led to a clash. A member of the Newfoundland constabulary was struck on the head with a club and critically injured. This clash lasted for some ten minutes. Nine of the apparent ringleaders were arrested and the balance dispersed into nearby brush. I am informed that two of the crowd of strikers were also injured, but the extent of their injuries is not known. The member of the Newfoundland constabulary is critically ill in hospital.
In concluding this statement, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make it clear that I have made this report to the house not because I as Attorney General of Canada have any immediate responsibility for the enforcement of law and order in the province of Newfoundland, but simply in my capacity as minister responsible for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. As such it is my concern to see that the police discharge their responsibilities wherever they may arise, and it is also my concern to investigate any criticism of the conduct of the R.C.M. police. I have investigated and reported upon the situation accordingly.
I	am satisfied from my investigation that there is no foundation for any suggestion that the police have permitted themselves to be

used as strikebreakers. I am also satisfied that they have acted strictly within the limits of their duties in connection with the enforcement of the criminal law as these duties are multiplied under the circumstances of a strike. Indeed, it is apparent that the approximately 150 police involved have done a thoroughly creditable job in their efforts to preserve the peace over a long period under most trying and difficult circumstances.

speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: UNRWA-GIFT OF FLOUR FOR PALESTINE REFUGEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the house will be interested in the statement I am about to make. The government has decided to seek parliamentary approval for a special gift of $1,500,000 worth of Canadian flour, which is equivalent to about
973,000	bushels of wheat, to the United Nations relief and works agency for Palestine

refugees. This proposed expenditure will be in addition to our normal cash contribution of $500,000 for which parliamentary approval will be asked when we consider the main estimates for 1959-60.
The house will recall that a similar special flour contribution was made to UNRWA last year. That contribution, together with a very large matching contribution made by the United States, we have been informed, brought about a considerable though temporary improvement in UNRWA's finances and, as we had hoped, the agency has been able to make plans to use the savings effected on food costs, through our gift of flour, to revive some of the more constructive rehabilitation projects of the agency such as improved vocational training facilities and the like. Some of these activities had to be abandoned because of lack of funds.
Recently, however, despite new and increased pledges by a number of countries and despite a lower total budget, UNRWA has again found itself gravely short of funds. As last year, our flour contribution will also make available to UNRWA a large additional contribution from the United States on a matching basis. The contribution is being made not only because of the humanitarian reasons which the government will place before the house but by reason also of UNRWA's important role in preserving political stability in the area through its relief and rehabilitation work among the refugees.
This special contribution is also evidence at this time of Canadian support for a proposal that was unanimously adopted by the United Nations assembly last year, namely to designate 1959 as a world refugee year. The objective of the world refugee year is to focus attention of governments and peoples on the unfortunate plight of large groups of refugees and, by drawing forth increased support for programs in their aid, to alleviate and where possible solve their difficulties.
Mr. Speaker, just for a moment I will seize this opportunity to speak of the contributions that have been made by Canadian citizens and certain voluntary organizations in Canada in addition to government help for UNRWA. A number of private Canadian charitable organizations are providing extremely valuable and worth-while assistance. The Unitarian service committee of Canada, for example, provided in 1958 some 20 tons of clothing for the refugees, 10,000 layettes sewn by thousands of groups across Canada, and funds for commercial and nurse-midwife training courses. Mr. Speaker, the announcement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs will be welcomed by all hon. members in this house. It is, of course, a continuation, as he would be the first to recognize, of a policy that was adopted a number of years ago by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) when he served as secretary of state for external affairs. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask a supplementary question. Has the Minister of Trade and Commerce any comment to make on the new and mandatory restrictions placed by the United States on imports of Canadian oil?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MANDATORY CONTROLS ON EXPORTS TO U.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Calgary South had spoken to me respecting this matter, and I wish to advise that, as hon. members are aware, the President of the United States yesterday proclaimed the institution of a system of mandatory controls on imports of petroleum and petroleum products. These replaced the voluntary oil import program which had been in effect since July, 1957, and which apparently had been fully considered prior to June 10, 1957, and the decision as to the course to be taken determined.

This note brings to the attention of Canadians a matter of grave concern to Canada. This government has vigorously and repeatedly protested the application to Canada of any United States restrictions on imports of oil, whatever their form. As was pointed out to the United States government in our recent note of February 19, we believe there is no justification on the ground of security, or for that matter on any other ground, for restrictions on oil imports from Canada.
The text of the new regulations has just been received; therefore there has not been time to study their implications. However, in his statement yesterday to the press the President referred to informal discussions which are taking place between Canada, Venezuela and the United States. The position of Canada was made clear to the United States cabinet secretaries at the meetings with them on January 5 and January 6. On January 19 and January 20 some of our of-ficals participated in informal discussions in Washington. On each and every one of these occasions it has been urged that whatever restrictive measures the United States found necessary to adopt, those measures should not apply to Canada.
In the course of his press statement yesterday the President indicated a desire that further conversations should be held. The government will seize every opportunity-and I want to make this very clear-to obtain unimpeded access to the United States market for Canadian oil. In this or in other ways which may be necessary our determination is to safeguard the interests of the Canadian oil industry.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: Is the minister not going to make a statement on introducing this resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of this resolution is very clear and


very simple. It is to extend for another year the increase which was made a year ago in the provincial share of the yield from the personal income tax from the 10 per cent rate which was established in the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act to 13 per cent. The whole subject of dominion-provincial fiscal relations was very fully discussed in this house in a two day debate on February 9 and 10. I take it there is no occasion to cover today ground that was then very fully covered.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance was extremely brief in introducing this resolution. However, in view of the fact that it relates to our federal system and our relationship with the provinces, notwithstanding the debate that we had on February 9 and 10, there is involved in the matter a great deal that the minister has not referred to. I would hope that before we pass this stage he will feel prompted to say something to the committee in explanation of some of the queries which I am sure are in the minds of a great number of members.
It is true that I was one of those who participated in that debate on February 10. In consideration of all of my colleagues I do not want to be unduly repetitive. On the other hand, under our rules the debate was limited by time and the minister was permitted to speak only once. Unlike the present occasion, he was not enabled to reply to subsequent questions, questions which are of very great merit. I hope that before we move on to the next stage we may get some further enlightenment from the minister. Despite what the minister may say it cannot be denied that we are again facing something that he himself was most vigorous in criticizing in the past, that is, any suggestion that in our dealings with the provinces there might be something in the nature of a unilateral decree. I cannot think of anything more deserving of the description, "unilateral decree", than the telegram type of notification the minister sent late in January of 1958.
I feel that this particular subject is very deserving of the attention of the committee because I am quite sure that in the last few days the minister is finding-the evidence has been put before some of the rest of us also-that there is quite a harvest of disenchantment with respect to the equation of promises with performance. I cannot think of any area where this is more noticeable than in the matter of federal-provincial relationships.
As I have said before, and I think it is worth repeating, in this new parliament we have a great number of members who were

not here when the basic statute was introduced in 1956. At that time the Minister of Finance, who is introducing the measure now before us, and the present Prime Minister had a great deal to say. I am quite sure that members of the house, including the heavily weighted government party, are fully aware of the promises of the Prime Minister in both the 1957 and 1958 campaigns. But I am not so sure that one could expect them to be equally familiar with the positions taken and the commitments made by the present Minister of Finance and Prime Minister when federal-provincial relations were discussed in 1956.
When we had an opportunity to debate this matter in 1956 at this very stage, the first speech made by a member of the opposition was made by the then leader of the opposition, Mr. Drew. He took violent exception to proceeding with a matter that had a great effect upon our provinces in the absence of what he thought was adequate consultation with those provinces. I am going to speak about consultation with the provinces but I want to draw to the attention of the committee, particularly to the attention of new members, what I think is a very decided contrast in what we are being asked to do today.
On July 16, 1956, during debate on the resolution stage, the very same stage we are in at the moment, Mr. Drew had this to say with respect to the proposals of the previous government as to tax sharing, as found on page 5999 of Hansard:
A government that fails to seek a solution of this problem and puts this matter into rigid statutory form before there has been approval is a government that is unfit to govern.
A year has elapsed since we were asked to do exactly what we are asked to do today. When the present Minister of Finance was in opposition in 1956, in his usual vigorous manner he had some very stern criticisms to make of the procedure, and I want to recall his words to his mind today. With respect to the matter of whether or not we have got the cart before the horse, the Minister of Finance had this to say as found on page 6296 of Hansard for July 23, 1956:
A new conference . . . is . . . desirable. There is no use. so far as Her Majesty's loyal opposition is concerned, asking us to approve a form of dominion-provincial fiscal arrangement which has not received the approval of a single provincial government.
Before we conclude debate at this stage I think the minister should indicate whether or not his views have changed in this respect. The minister went further on second reading. I do not want to anticipate that stage, but on February 10 the minister felt that the 66968-9-117
Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act statute itself was undesirable, unwise and was incomprehensible. He described it as a maze. Yet when he amended the statute last year he simply wanted to make one slight change. He said that where the statute then read "10 per cent'' it should from then on read "13 per cent". There were no alterations to remedy those things which he described in the most derogatory terms when he was sitting on this side of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext: I think my hon. friend should be fair enough to recognize that in the meantime agreements had been signed by nine provinces with the federal government under the terms of that legislation. We are not the kind of people who propose to repudiate such agreements.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
I am coming to that very point. My main point is that 24 months ago he and his leader assured the country in the election campaign of 1957 that there was nothing they were more concerned about if they were given the responsibility of administration than calling the provinces together and arriving at something that would not be a unilateral decree, as he described it, but on the contrary would be something that would result in benign satisfaction to all concerned.
I simply want to make the contrast I indicated earlier between the arrangements that were made before the introduction of this taxation statute in 1956 and what preceded the introduction of the minister's amendment in 1958, now repeated here. As I said, at that time the present Minister of Finance, the present Prime Minister and the then leader of the opposition were so vigorous in their criticism that they said any government was unfit to govern if it introduced a statute without being able to tell the house that it met with the approval of the other participants, the ten provincial governments.
What is the history of the taxation proposal of 1956? In April of 1955 there was a federal-provincial conference. It was followed by a conference in October. The then prime minister of the country had the courtesy to send to all those associated with him in the conference a very informative and descriptive indication of the thinking of the federal government resulting from the two conferences. There was no telegram, none of this "brinkmanship" which we saw last January when the provinces were told so abruptly, "this is it, you have it and that is all." That was followed by a conference in March, 1956, and it was after all these preliminaries that the former government felt disposed to ask parliament to make certain changes in the federal-provincial tax-sharing arrangements.

Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act
At each of these stages the record shows that as a result of the friendly consultation between the federal government and the provinces certain amendments or certain changes were made beneficial to the provinces beyond what might have been the position taken at the first conference on the part of the federal government. I will be most sympathetic to the Minister of Finance. In conference of this kind, with the bargaining that is involved in a matter of this kind, I do not think everybody can go away completely satisfied. However, what I am saying is that we had conferences and notwithstanding those conferences when in 1956 there was before this house the proposition that increased benefits to the provinces by 25 per cent, the Minister of Finance appearing with us again today was one of those who said that without proof that the provinces agreed to the proposition this parliament should not be asked to legislate by statute.
What is the contrast. I indicated that I felt that all hon. members would be quite familiar with the proposals of the Prime Minister in the last two election campaigns. I was unfortunately out of the chamber when the Minister of Finance introduced this resolution. I understand the minister took about 30 seconds to perform this task, and I find this rather strange remembering the minister's eloquence on other occasions when this same subject was under discussion. This resolution reads:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Federal - Provincial Tax - Sharing Arrangements Act to extend for a further period of one year the rate of 13 per cent for standard individual income tax for the purpose of calculating the tax equalization payments to the provinces and the amounts payable to the provinces under the tax rental agreements.
I must say that this resolution is an outstanding example of the tendency of the present government to conduct dominion-provincial relations on a unilateral basis, and certainly it reflects an approach which members of the Conservative party condemned in vigorous terms when they were in opposition. I think it will be appropriate at this time to place on the record some of the statements which were made by various members of the present cabinet on this subject. Let us take the Minister of Trade and Commerce, for example. That minister, speaking on July 7, 1956, as reported on page 6064 of Hansard, said:
The only way in which to approach this problem is by a conference which would deal with this crucial matter and deal with it not in 24 hours or in 48 hours but over a lengthy period.
Of course, we all recall that the conference which was called in the fall of 1957 lasted for only two days, November 25 and 26-

Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act Then again, the Minister of Justice, as reported on page 6335 of Hansard of July 23, 1956, had this to say:
What is needed is a meeting of all the governments with a view to assessing their needs and what if any exchange of constitutional responsibilities can be arranged by mutual consent.
I wonder what mutual consent there was about the telegrams which were sent out last January to inform the provinces what they were to receive, and, again, this year, when the announcement was made in the speech from the throne? What kind of mutual consent was there then? What steps were taken then to secure the consent of the provinces?
But in order to get a really good quotation we have to turn to the remarks of the Prime Minister himself as reported on page 6369 of Hansard of July 24, 1956 when he said:
I wonder often why this government has not taken the provinces into its confidence. Why these short-term meetings: why these gatherings of a day or two? Why do we not have a meeting of the federal authorities, the provincial authorities and the municipalities-designed to bring about the reconsideration of a problem which for the last 13 years or so has become increasingly complex?
I submit that the situation has become even more complex in the last couple of years. Then again, on July 24, 1956 the Prime Minister said these words as reported on page 6370:
I think it is fair to say that the attitude taken by the government at the last conference was an arbitrary one. The government simply said, "These are the terms". No opportunity was given for amendment or for amelioration of any term. The recipe for a division of taxation was as final as the laws of the Medes and Persians; and how similar that attitude was to the attitude of the government in the house which is that power makes perfect anything they do. There was no opportunity for negotiation; there was simply the attitude of a feudal lord bringing into being a modern feudalism and laying down the law to the vassals.
That is not the attitude, that is not the consideration to which the provinces are entitled under a constitution which allocates powers as between the federal and provincial governments.
How well those words could apply to the present government even more than they applied to the previous government. Then, of course, we come to what was said by the Minister of Finance. Speaking on July 23, 1956, as reported on page 6287, the hon. member for Eglinton had this to say:
The house is now asked to carry into legislative form and effect the formula which was the essence of the federal government's proposals. We are asked to do so with full knowledge that no provincial government has yet given its approval to those proposals and indeed with full knowledge that there has been widespread disapproval of the government's proposals on the ground of their inadequacy.

It seems so strange in the light of these words of the minister, spoken less than three years ago, to find now that the federal government's terms should be made known by telegram. And the Minister of Finance, speaking in the same debate, as reported on page 6289, said further:
-this rigid and inflexible, this hard take-it-or-leave-it attitude, is foreign to the spirit of confederation, and there has been altogether too much of that rigidity and inflexibility in the attitude of this government all through the years during which the problem of dominion-provincial fiscal relations has occupied the attention of all those governing the dominion and the provinces.
Certainly we can see very little difference between the attitude of the previous government and the attitude of the present government. If anything the attitude of the present government is worse than that of the former administration.
When the Prime Minister convened the dominion-provincial conference in 1956 he is quoted as having said:
We are not placing before you any take-it-or-leave-it attitudes. We are not taking any fast and hard positions.
From my observations of the present government I agree that it does not take hard and fast positions simultaneously; it takes them separately. I noticed that it took a very fast position when it came to increasing by 50 per cent the money accruing to moneylenders in this country but it reserves hard positions for the sake of the western farmers and the employees of Avro who were thrown out on the street.
We cannot criticize too severely the failure of the government to introduce proposals at the last dominion-provincial conference because it had been in office for only a few months. I do not know just how the impression was created or the undertaking given but it was clearly understood by the provinces on that occasion that the conference would be reconvened the following January in order to work out a satisfactory agreement between the federal and provincial governments. As we all know that January came and went and another January has come and gone and it is going on to a year and a half since the last conference concluded. Not only have we not had a conference but there is no indication of one in the offing.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE

Mr. Chairman, I thank you for your ruling and I shall endeavour to keep my remarks well within the rules. The proposal before us at this time is a continuation of the proposal introduced last year when an amendment was made to the tax-sharing formula which provided an increase from 10 per cent to 13 per cent in the standard individual income tax in computing provincial payments under the taxsharing agreement. The provinces were given no opportunity to discuss this proposal or to suggest amendments or alternative proposals. The federal government indicated that this was to be an interim measure effective for a period of one year but now the government is proposing that the present arrangement be extended for another one-year period without having consulted the provinces and with full knowledge that the provinces do not consider this formula adequate. This attitude of the government is most certainly representative of the take-it-or-leave-it attitude which hon. members of this administration so vehemently condemned while in opposition.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River made reference to the rosy picture that
Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act was painted by the Minister of Finance at the time this arrangement was introduced. This would be an increase only if the revenue stayed the same as before or if it were increased. What was accomplished was that the government raised the ceiling but did not raise the floor. A certain amount of optimism should be allowed to the government from time to time but I suggest that there has been an excess of optimism which is particularly noticeable on the part of the Minister of Finance. Many of the announcements made by that hon. gentleman lead us to believe that the country is being administered through the processes of government by mirage rather than through the processes of a government that bases its activities on facts and figures.
Possibly I have said enough concerning the actions of the government in the past. What I believe is of concern to Canadians as a whole is what the government will do in future. Will it continue to wallow in the same bog of indecision which characterized the previous administration which fact was so frequently and vocally deplored by hon. gentlemen opposite when they were in opposition? On the other hand will the government clear the decks and endeavour to establish a reasonable and just understanding with respect to these matters that would prevail from coast to coast?
Eight years from now in 1967 Canada will celebrate the 100th anniversary of its founding. Certainly that would be an excellent time to conduct a complete review of the situation in the country in order that each segment could contribute its full share to our development and perform its proper duties. It is essential that the federal government should retain its taxing powers so it can maintain the responsibility of establishing monetary and fiscal policies throughout the country. The taxing field should be left to the federal government. If this were not done how could it possibly meet national emergencies? It would have no money with which to meet these problems if the taxing authority was removed from its hands.
On the other hand the provinces have grown to have responsibilities that were not even dreamed of in 1867. They require federal assistance to meet their growing responsibilities. This line of thinking is not new. May I refer to a statement made by the former hon. member for Dauphin, Mr. Zaplitny, as reported at page 6333 of Hansard of July 23, 1956:
If there were a constitutional conference, and if those who participated took a good look at things, had expert advice, decided what from now on could be more efficiently handled on the provincial level and what in the national interests could be more efficiently handled on the federal level, and

Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act then suggested to parliament and eventually to the parliament of Westminster further amendments to our constitution based upon the results of that conference and arising out of common agreement among the representatives of the provinces and the dominion, we would do away with a great many of the difficulties that arise at a time when we are wondering how best to share these revenues.
I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the. measure before the house now is more a matter of expediency than it is of any particular benefit. In fact, more and more people in this country are beginning to believe that the policy of this government is nothing more nor less than what the Prime Minister says is expedient to do each morning when he rises. That becomes the policy of the present government. If we are going to accept the responsibilities in this country of ours we cannot and we must not permit this to continue. I would say, let us fix 1967 as the target date for maturity in this country. One of the biggest steps in that direction would be to make some honest effort to solve this problem which unfortunately this government appears to have avoided so far.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in introducing the measure under discussion this afternoon the Minister of Finance was exceptionally brief. He stated that the purpose of this resolution was clear and simple and all that it intended to do was to extend for another year the federal-provincial taxsharing arrangements which were passed in this house last year.
In introducing the measure amending the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act last year on January 27 the Minister of Finance made it clear to the house that this act provided an interim measure only and that in its application to the fiscal year commencing on April 1, 1958, the definition of "standard individual income tax" in the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act shall for the purposes of that act and any agreements made thereunder be read and construed as if for the words "10 per cent" therein there were substituted the words "13 per cent". As I have just said, the resolution before us at the present time resolves:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Federal - Provincial Tax - Sharing Arrangements Act to extend the present act for a further period of one year-
This is an interim measure. In fact, Mr. Chairman, it is really in accordance with the present government's policy, which is a short term policy of introducing interim measures after interim measures.
On January 27 of last year, in introducing the resolution which provided the extension

from 10 per cent to 13 per cent of the individual income tax share of the equalization formula under the federal-provincial fiscal arrangements, the Minister of Finance said, as reported at page 3847 of Hansard:
Mr. Chairman, to the present resolution and to the bill which it is hoped will follow upon the passage of the resolution, the government attaches very great importance, for it looks upon this measure as one that will bring aid to the provinces and municipalities of this country, and effective also in meeting the problem of unemployment. The terms of the resolution. I think, are clear. It is the hope of the government that it may be possible after adoption of this resolution to proceed with the motion for second reading of the bill tomorrow.
I will agree with the minister that the terms of the resolution are clear, and I think the government looked upon this measure as one which should bring aid to the provinces and the municipalities of this country. The present economic condition of the provinces and municipalities justifies the need for more than an extension of the present tax-sharing arrangements for a period of one year. In the report of the proceedings of the dominion-provincial conference of November 19, 1957 we find at page 5, the foreward of the report, the following quotation:
It was agreed at the end of the conference that a subsequent meeting be held as soon as possible in the new year in accordance with the proposals made by the federal government in calling the conference.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, this report makes it very clear that it was the intention of the government to call a dominion-provincial conference at a later date early in the new year. It was made clear that a subsequent meeting would be held as soon as possible in accordance with the proposals. In tabling on behalf of the Prime Minister copies of telegrams dispatched by the Prime Minister to the premiers of the 10 provinces on the matter of dominion-provincial fiscal relations, which we are discussing today, on January 25 of last year the Minister of Finance is reported at page 3796 of Hansard for that date to have said:
It has not been possible, as we had hoped it would be, to reconvene the dominion-provincial conference in January. Therefore as an interim measure, and an interim measure only, we are asking parliament immediately to make available this additional sum of money for the forthcoming fiscal year. Then when there is opportunity it is the intention of the government to reconvene the dominion-provincial conference with a view, as indicated in the letter, to seeking fiscal settlements. This was put forward, of course, without prejudice to the freedom that the dominion-provincial conference will undoubtedly have to discuss the whole area of fiscal settlements.

The telegram which was read and inserted in Hansard on January 25, 1958, as reported at page 3795, said in part:
This is interim measure pending reconvening of dominion-provincial conference to seek fiscal settlements.
These are exactly the same words as were used by the Minister of Finance. The last sentence of this telegram signed by the Prime Minister reads as follows:
The government of Canada hopes this additional assistance aggregating eighty-seven million dollars in fiscal year commencing April first will be useful in helping provinces and municipalities to meet unemployment and other problems.
There again, Mr. Chairman, it was made clear that this measure, which we are asked to renew today for another period of 12 months, was introduced as an interim measure only, pending the reconvening of the dominion-provincial conference in January of last year. Last year the session which was then under way ended on January 31. An election was held and it was followed by a second session of parliament which ended on September 7. Over a year has since gone by and today we are being asked by the Minister of Finance, not to make an improvement in the act or in the arrangements which we were asked to pass last year but just to extend the same agreement for a period of another year. In repeating his pledge to distribute more federal revenues to the provinces and municipalities the Prime Minister said at St. Patrice de Beaurivage on May 30, 1957, as reported in the Montreal Gazette for May 31:
The provinces and municipalities are poor but the Ottawa government is rich.
Would it be true that conditions have changed considerably since May, 1957, because in June of 1957 a Conservative government took office in Ottawa? Would it be true that the federal treasury may not be in as healthy a state today as it was when the present government took over the administration of the affairs of the country? The fact remains, however, that the Prime Minister promised to make sure that the provinces and municipalities would have sufficient money to do the job they are supposed to do, and notwithstanding the charges which have been made on previous occasions in the house by the Minister of Finance blaming us of accusing the Prime Minister of not keeping his promises, we of the official opposition will make it our duty to remind the Prime Minister and his followers of the promises which they have made to the electors of the country, promises made to provinces and to municipalities, promises which they claim to have fulfilled but with respect to which the results so far are pretty insignificant.
Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act
I wonder if any individual member on the government side could go before his constituents today and convince them that the promises made by the Prime Minister to the provinces and the municipalities have been fulfilled. I hear one hon. member say, "We could." Well, just for his information I will recall some of the statements which have been made by the Prime Minister in this regard. I recall first the statement made by the Prime Minister at a press conference in Winnipeg on May 14, 1957, when he said, as reported in the Winnipeg Free Press:
The provinces have been placed in a starving condition. The municipalities have been placed in a position where property owners are laced with heavy burdens of taxation.
We all know that starving conditions were prominent in this country during the last Conservative government, the Bennett regime. Was the statement of the Prime Minister made on May 14, 1957 a prediction of worse days to come? Did he have a premonition at that time of the conditions which exist in Canada today after only 20 months of Conservative government?
The Minister of Finance clearly stated that the government had carried the principle of equalization further than any previous government. The fact is that only 12 or 13 months after the introduction of an amendment to the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act the government is already forced to back away from the principle established by the last amendment. In fact, when the estimates for the coming fiscal year were tabled in the house a few weeks ago it was revealed that six provinces will receive considerably less under the tax-sharing agreements than they received during the present fiscal year, and unfortunately the provinces most affected under the new agreement are those which are recognized as being the needy provinces.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
The Prime Minister stated time and time again that the tax-sharing pattern used by the previous Liberal administration was niggardly so far as the provinces and municipalities were concerned. If the pattern was niggardly then when conditions were normal what must it be today when over 12 per cent of our national labour force are unemployed and seeking work?
It is true that the interim measure introduced in January, 1958, and the extension we are being asked to ratify today increased from 10 per cent to 13 per cent the individual tax share which the provinces will receive from the federal treasury. However, by failing to place a floor on the amounts which each province will receive, let us say based on the 1957-58 levels as asked last year by the then member for Montmagny-L'Islet, Mr. Lesage, the 1959 estimates now show, notwithstanding the denial of the Minister of Finance, that the poor provinces, the provinces which need it most today, may receive in the coming fiscal year substantially less than they were allotted for the year 1958-59 under the equalization method.
In fact, according to the figures we find in the estimates, to which I have just referred, New Brunswick, for example, is estimated to receive close to three-quarters of a million dollars less and Nova Scotia over $1,400,000 less and this at a time when unemployment in those provinces is at a record high, in fact, almost as high as during the hungry 30's. We are prepared to admit that the provinces were not completely satisfied with the fiscal arrangements made under the previous administration and they are definitely not satisfied with the present arrangements.
At the short 1958 conference which lasted only two days every provincial premier, without exception, asked for a more favourable tax-sharing agreement or more adequate fiscal arrangements. As late as March 26, 1958, as reported in the Halifax Herald for March 27, premier Stanfield, addressing a political meeting at Tatamagouche, said:
Unless the tax-sharing agreements between the federal and provincial governments were revised substantially, our revenues from Ottawa would fall sharply. Nova Scotia, he said, was in no position to absorb such a reduciton.
This is in fact exactly what will happen during the coming fiscal year, and it is one of the reasons why the convening of a

federal-provincial conference is urgent and the extension of the present arrangement for the period of one year will not be satisfactory. The former leader of the Conservative party, Mr. George Drew, when leader of the opposition and while addressing the house on July 16, 1956, clearly stated, as found on page 5993 of Hansard, that an arrangement should be made to reallocate to provincial governments and municipalities their share of taxes "which will make it possible for them to carry out the heavy responsibilities which they cannot ignore and cannot shirk."
I am sure that Mr. Frost, the premier of Ontario, would be pleased to hear those words repeated today. In the course of the same debate the present Solicitor General addressed the house and had this to say, as found at page 6031 of Hansard:
What is most required is a federal-provincial conference in which the federal government and the provinces will consider the steps to be taken for a fair distribution of taxation fields so that the provinces may play their part in their own sphere.
I am sure that Premier Duplessis would be pleased to hear those words repeated today. At a press conference in Winnipeg on May 14, 1957 the Prime Minister stated that "under a Conservative government the provinces would have a voice in deciding fiscal terms and the tax agreements would contribute to national unity". Where is that voice today? Has it faded because a Conservative government is in power in Ottawa? I am sure that the premier of Manitoba, Mr. Roblin, would be pleased to have those words repeated today. A few days later in Victoria the Prime Minister said this:
The time has come for a meeting of the provinces with the municipalities present, to discuss their problems. He intended, said the Prime Minister, to convene such a meeting in the spirit of confederation.
Again I am sure that Premier Bennett would be glad to hear those words repeated today. Here is a further statement of the Prime Minister when he said this:
If action is not taken, we shall find ourselves in a position in five years' time where the municipalities will be bankrupt or unable to carry out their responsibilities.
It did not take five years, Mr. Chairman, under a Conservative government for the prediction of the Prime Minister to be realized. The present government has been in power less than 20 months and already throughout the country numbers of municipalities are on the verge of bankruptcy or are unable to carry out their responsibilities. Where is the action promised by the Prime Minister to ease the present tax burdens of municipalities? Where is the action promised by the Prime Minister at the opening of the

short 1957 dominion-provincial conference when, in addressing the provincial premiers, as reported at pages 8 and 9 of the report, he said:
When we have your views and suggestions we would like to study them in detail and prepare some specific proposals to put before you at a mutually convenient time in the new year. This would be in accordance with the experience in one or other past conferences, and I believe it is the most acceptable procedure and the only feasible one under all the circumstances.
Mr. Chairman, the 1958 new year has passed and the 1959 new year is passing. Yet we are still waiting for the conference and we have no indication whatsoever-

historical reasons which has been given ever since the days of the Rowell-Sirois report on the principle of tax-sharing is that the provinces, and through them the municipalities, should be put in a financial position to carry out their functions. My hon. friend from Gloucester is showing, or attempting to show, that in his province, in one of the leading municipalities, the present arrangements which this government is asking to be continued are not being so continued. taken, I would like to quote from Beauchesne's fourth edition, page 126, rule 148 (1), which states:
It is a wholesome restraint upon members that they cannot revive a debate already concluded; and it would be little use in preventing the same question from being offered twice in the same session if, without being offered, its merits might be discussed again and again.
Consequently, I must defer to the point of order which the Minister of Finance raises, and that is that we cannot return to a debate on which there has been a vote. It would be appreciated by the Chair if the hon. members of the house confined their remarks as much as possible to the item under debate.

maintopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL TAX-SHARING ARRANGEMENTS ACT FURTHER EXTENSION OF INCOME TAX RATE
speechtext:
The Prime Minister in Truro on May 1, 1957 promised that the Conservative government would immediately convene a dominion-provincial conference with representatives of the provinces and municipalities to restore once again the opportunity for provinces and municipalities to exercise their functions under the terms of confederation. Direct taxation in the different municipalities of the province of New Brunswick has reached its limit. Some of those counties may certainly be a good section of the country to live in, but we have reached the point where it is impossible to live and expect the same privileges as enjoyed in other sections of the country. I do not want to cite any specific examples concerning my municipality of Gloucester but, for example, owning a car in Canada is not ordinarily considered a luxury. In some counties in the province of New Brunswick the owner of a car has to pay from $36 to $70 a year municipal taxes if it is a small imported car like an Austin, or any of the others of similar make. If he is the owner of what we call a standard car, like a Ford or a Chevrolet, his municipal taxes are $54 to $110 a year. If he is the owner of a larger car, like a Buick or Monarch, his taxes are from $100 to $200 a year. I am not blaming our municipal councillors, because these gentlemen are doing the impossible to meet the existing demands of their respective municipalities. But nevertheless the situation is beyond their control and they have no other field of taxation from which to raise the funds required for the administration of their municipalities. This is why we feel that the purpose of the amendment which we are being asked to discuss and pass today would not meet the needs of the different municipalities.
I realize that there may not be permanent and realistic solution to the complex problems of fiscal relations. However, I feel that practical compromises should be marked out to meet changing social and economic conditions which also affect the responsibilities
Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act of the federal, provincial and municipal governments. Every Canadian citizen is entitled to a certain reasonable minimum of services without having to bear a level of taxation more onerous than the average Canadian. All across Canada municipalities are finding their tax revenues inadequate for the rapidly mounting cost of their operations. Money is getting more and more expensive and difficult to obtain. During the last four or five years municipal expenditures have increased by over 50 per cent. The cost of financing education, health, welfare, roads, utility services and others have increased year after year. Some provinces, like Manitoba, have made available to municipalities a large share of the amount received under fiscal grants, or under federal-provincial tax arrangements, while others, like New Brunswick for example, have refused to recognize the urgent needs of municipal governments.
This is a clear example of unilateral decision where the municipalities did not have one word to say. The municipalities face the most critical conditions of all levels of government, and the municipalities are faced with the most widespread demands for expenditure; but they have nothing to say in getting their right share of amounts paid under federal-provincial fiscal arrangements. The federal government could also arrange for municipalities to borrow at a lower rate of interest, somewhere in the vicinity of the federal rate. Mr. Chairman, I am happy to take part in this debate in order to remind the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) that he must now fulfil a promise he made during the last election in the province of Quebec, and which as a matter of fact, he had already held out in July 1956, when we were discussing the matter in this house. Here is what the Minister of Finance said in July 1956, as can be seen on page 6296 of the official record dated July 23rd 1956:
I ask the government to take a responsible attitude in this matter and recognize the imperative needs of the provincial and municipal governments. This formula is at best a makeshift; it is no solution of the problem. What is needed is a government with a realistic and sympathetic appreciation of the responsibilities and burdens and problems of the provinces and a wholesome respect for the constitutional position of the provinces and the constitutional rights they possess, as well as the responsibilities they bear.
Moreover, during the 1958 election campaign, the Minister of Finance came to the province of Quebec, and more particularly to

Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act my riding, on March 17th or 24th of last year, and, speaking on behalf of my opponent, Mr. Danis, he promised the final settlement of this issue with the province of Quebec. I am aware that the minister is a man of integrity, of talent, and a glutton for work, but I shall tell him that, when he promised to settle the problem of fiscal relations with the province of Quebec, he undertook a very hard task indeed.
At the 1957 conference, a meeting of the provinces had been called to explore their needs. They were then promised a further conference where the government would state its position.
I have no intention of repeating the statements made by previous speakers, but I can say to the Minister of Finance that, to settle a problem of such magnitude, he needs the co-operation of the authorities concerned.
When he proposes, as he now does, to grant to provinces, and particularly to the province of Quebec, 13 per cent of federal income tax, I say as other members have said that this is a poor solution as far as the province of Quebec is concerned.
I said just now that, to correct the situation and settle the problem, he needs the co-operation of the parties concerned. However, I wonder whether he can hope for the Quebec government to co-operate in this matter. If we look up the proceedings of the 1955 conference, on page 40, and the proceedings of the 1957 conference on page 31, we find that the premier of Quebec came to Ottawa to repeat the same thing in both circumstances. I quote his statement:
1.	Clarification and delimitation of the powers of taxation of both the federal and provincial authorities, in accordance with the letter and spirit of the Canadian constitution, that is to say having regard to the past, the present and the future.
2.	Simplification of public taxation in such a way as to reduce its cost and facilitate its collection.
3.	Moderation in the domain of taxation to be arrived at by the collaboration of all public powers, in such a way as to ease the burden of the taxpayer so far as possible.
Those sentences were repeated at both conferences, and it is obvious that the necessary co-operation for the settlement of such a vast problem will not be easy to get.
The situation, in the province of Quebec, is quite special. If the Minister of Finance wants to settle the problem, he will have many prejudices to overcome, not because of the stubbornness of the premier of Quebec, but rather because of his puns and of his distorted mind.
Only a few days ago I heard the premier of Quebec say that the federal government was grabbing 75 per cent of taxes. However,
[Mr. Meunier.l

he made no mention of the equalization payments or of all that the province of Quebec receives under the constitution, or what the province gets in the form of grants for hospitals and for professional and technical schools. Without explaining the exact situation he prefers to insinuate that the federal government grabs 75 per cent of taxes, instead of saying that the federal government collects taxes and offers in turn the equalization payments, as is the case now. For the year 1957-58, the province of Quebec received $51,815,000 and this year, it will receive $55,809,000, and this is not taking into account the other amounts paid under certain statutes.
We are sure that the federal government is not grabbing 75 per cent of the tax dollar; it levies those taxes and then hands them back to the provinces. I then say to the Minister of Finance, Mr. Chairman, that he has a mission to fulfil, because in the province of Quebec the story goes-and people believe it-that the fiscal agreements of 1956 were agreed to with a knife held to the provinces' throats, and that the provinces, especially the province of Quebec, were forced to accept what was offered them.
Furthermore, during the last election campaigns, the Minister of Finance kept repeating that he would settle the problem to the satisfaction of all, as the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) also claimed here, for instance on October 18, 1957, when in reply to a question put to him by a member of the opposition, he stated:
I wish to tell my hon. friend that I am still opposed to subsidies such as were proposed by the former government.
And later on, he added:
I want to tell him that the proposals of the federal government are not yet known, but I am convinced that they will be made on a very different basis from those of the former government.
I understand the Solicitor General was not then speaking on behalf of the government, but what he said squares with what the Minister of Finance stated on various occasions, i.e. that the problem of fiscal relations would be solved fully and satisfactorily, in so far as the provinces, especially the province of Quebec, are concerned.
I am not reproaching him for his failure to call another conference, but I hope that within a year he will have called one and thus given satisfaction to the province of Quebec, since its population is now being deprived of considerable and badly needed income.

I wish to make brief reference to interest rates as they apply to a couple of municipalities in British Columbia. I choose these only because they are representative of the general pattern. I take this information from the 1958 red book on British Columbia municipal statistics which I have in my hand. These figures relate to borrowings guaranteed by the province of British Columbia and they would therefore bear a lower interest rate than would debenture issues floated by municipalities without such guarantees on the part of the province.
In 1947 the village of Burns Lake issued 20-year debentures at an interest rate of 3 per cent which even today would be a pretty high rate to have to pay. Eleven years later the same village issued 20-year debentures in the same amount and for the same purpose but the interest rate was jacked up to 4 per cent. The interest on the borrowings of another village municipality, Lumby, for 1958, was 5 per cent. That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act to extend lor a further period of one year the rate of 13 per cent for standard individual income tax for the purpose of calculating the tax equalization payments to the provinces and the amounts payable to the provinces under the tax rental agreements.
We are placed in the position of being asked to agree as to whether or not we should allow the provinces to have a little more money for one more year. I say that this resolution is inadequate; it is completely inadequate. I had hoped that after all the election campaigns, after all the pledges and
Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act after all the promises of the new deal that we have heard so much about, the minister would have introduced a resolution that certainly would have given a bit of indication of the new deal. However, in my opinion this resolution is something that is based upon expediency. This resolution contains no indication of the new deal for the lower levels of government that we have heard so much about over a goodly number of years now.
I am sure that in 1867 the fathers of confederation had no idea of what the functions of the various levels of government might be like in the year 1959. They made arrangements to meet the particular time and circumstances that they were faced with at that time. Today the function of the federal government and its responsibilities are relatively small in the light of the developing and growing responsibilities facing the municipal and provincial levels of government. The Conservative party pledged itself to do something to remedy the situation if the electors would elect it to office. I can well remember the Conservative party when in opposition moving an amendment calling for a rearrangement of the existing situation, in so far as the responsibilities, and especially in their opinion in so far as the revenues of the various levels of government were concerned.
I have obtained a little bit of information and I find that in the year 1958 the revenues of the federal government from only three tax fields amounted to $3,001.8 million. I hasten to add that these were not by any means the only sources of revenue of the federal government; the revenues of the federal government were much higher indeed. However, from only three main sources the federal government collected $3,001.8 million and the net revenues of all the 10 provincial governments of Canada totalled only $2,051 million. I am informed that in that year, taking all the taxes that the people of Canada paid, the federal government received 75 cents out of every dollar. Our provincial governments received 11 cents out of the tax dollar, and while many of us think that municipal taxes are very high, and they are, municipal governments were able to collect only 14 cents out of the tax dollar. In other words, the federal government collected 75 per cent, the lion's share of the tax payments of the Canadian people and the other levels of government had to be satisfied with a mere 25 per cent or with taking only one dollar out of every four.
It is hardly good enough that a new government pledged to a new deal should now ask the house to renew once again the old and inadequate arrangement arrived at in the past. The minister may well attempt to

Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act argue that he gave the provinces more money. Yet I think he will have to admit that statistics have proved that actually he did not give them any more money, that actually they are in receipt of less money than they received on other occasions.

I do not think the minister expected at that time that events and circumstances in the year ahead would be such as to eliminate most of the $65 million increase announced by him.
We in our group realized at the time what was happening on the Canadian economic scene and we feel that the minister's advisers should have advised him that the increase of $65 million announced by the minister would at best only result in a very small increase to some provinces and in the case of others the result would be that they would actually receive less money than on other occasions.
The resolution before us is in very specific terms. The minister is asking that the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act be extended for one year. Surely that is far from satisfactory. If the minister feels that the existing formula is so realistic and has to be continued then he should be able to give the provinces some indication of what kind of a deal they can expect beyond one year. Our provincial governments have to do a lot of planning if they hope to meet their constitutional responsibilities and it is hardly satisfactory for the minister to ask the provinces to be satisfied with what is in effect an ad hoc arrangement whereby he says to them, "Let us go from month to month and see how we get along". Our provincial governments need more assurance than that.
I have mentioned how the federal government takes in much more money, although only from three tax fields, than do the ten provincial governments combined. However, I might take another approach to this matter. The responsibilities of the other levels of government have grown tremendously. The share of the tax dollar of the senior level of government has grown but at the same time its share of responsibility has, in the absence of war, declined substantially. Therefore we now have a situation where one government,

with a smaller percentage of responsibility than before, has the lion's share of the tax dollar while the other levels of government, whose percentage of responsibility has grown by leaps and bounds because of our changing society, find that their share of tax revenue has declined year by year.

Born in Brantford, Ontario, in 1915, he attended Parkdale Collegiate Institute, Toronto, and the University of Toronto, where he took his B.A. with honours in philosophy and psychology in 1938. Later, at the University of Oxford where he was a Rhodes scholar, be specialized in philosophy with particular emphasis on aesthetics. He also held a fellowship at the Institute of Fine Arts, New York University, New York, and took additional graduate studies in art history at the University of Toronto. During the war he worked in the aircraft industry in England on training and industrial relations. In 1945, he was private secretary to the late Sir Stafford Cripps, who was then president of the board of trade in the United Kingdom government. His great interest in design took him after the war to the newly organized council of industrial design in England and he became its first public relations officer; he handled the publicity for the "Britain Can Make It" exhibition in 1946 which first brought contemporary British design to the attention of the post-war world. Later he became executive director of Pilgrim Films,

an independent film producing organization. From 1951 he was head of Oxford House in London, England. While residing in England he was actively engaged is many cultural activities including the post of editor of a series of design booklets "The Things We See" published by Penguin Books. He is a sculptor with works in collections in Canada and the United States and he has written and lectured widely in art and design. His cultural interests include drama and the stage and prior to returning to Canada in 1951 he was chairman of the board of governors of the Group theatre in London.
